question: Of the components one has to get right to train a large language model, which ones did university research mostly concentrate on until around 2023, and which ones are argued to decide the outcome in practice?
points: Until about 2023 most academic work went into the model architecture and the training algorithm / loss.
In practice the three that matter are data (how much and how clean), evaluation (knowing whether you are making progress) and systems/infrastructure for scaling up.
Architecture is treated as the less important part because it has stopped changing much: open models mostly use transformers with mixture of experts.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the Hugging Face study that shows how cleaning a raw web crawl improves pre-training, how many tokens were left after the first round of filters and after deduplication, and what counted as too many copies?
points: The raw crawl was about 200 trillion tokens; the first filters (unsafe-content blocklist, mostly English only, simple document checks such as repetition and length) left about 36 trillion.
Deduplication cut that by nearly half, to about 20 trillion tokens.
The rule was not to keep text that is duplicated more than about 100 times (the targets were huge clusters, e.g. 100,000 copies).
Training on the deduplicated data scores better, because the model is not made to learn repeated, uninformative content.
author: fable-5.2

question: What does the well-known study on dividing a fixed training-compute budget between a bigger model and more data recommend, and why can it be the wrong guide for a company that serves the model to many users?
points: It finds that the training-optimal balance is roughly 20 training tokens per model parameter.
It only optimises the training resources needed to reach a given training loss and leaves inference cost out.
A larger model costs more per user at inference time, so training a smaller model for longer can be preferable even though it takes more training compute for the same performance.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why can supervised fine-tuning on answers that are themselves correct still teach a language model to fabricate, and which example is used to show it?
points: Supervised fine-tuning is behaviour cloning: the model is trained to copy the given output.
The problem arises when the target answer contains something the model itself does not know to be true (it was not in what it learned during pre-training), even though the answer is correct.
Example: an answer that cites a reference unknown to the model; the model is thereby taught to produce plausible-looking references whether or not it knows they exist.
author: fable-5.2

question: In mixed-precision training of large models, what is kept in 32-bit floating point and what is done in 16-bit, and why is the lower precision considered both worthwhile and harmless?
points: The weights are stored in 32-bit; they are converted to 16-bit (BF16) before the computation, the computation and the gradients are in 16-bit, and the result is put back into the 32-bit weights so that small updates still register.
It is worthwhile because the GPU bottleneck is memory and communication rather than the arithmetic: fewer bits per value means less memory and faster data movement.
It is harmless because exact decimal precision matters little in deep learning apart from a few operations: training with stochastic gradient descent is already noisy.
author: fable-5.2

question: When a model is copied onto several GPUs that each process a different slice of the batch, what is gained and what is not, and how does splitting the training state across the GPUs address the shortfall?
points: Each GPU holds a full copy of the model and optimizer, works on its own part of the data, and the gradients are summed; the gain is speed in proportion to the number of GPUs (four GPUs, four times faster).
Nothing is saved in memory: every GPU still needs the full training state (112 GB for a 7-billion-parameter model), so a model that did not fit on one GPU still does not fit.

Sharding (the ZeRO approach) has each GPU hold only a subset of the optimizer states, and likewise of gradients and parameters, communicating them when needed; sharding the optimizer states alone cuts the example from about 120 GB to about 31 GB, nearly four times less.
author: fable-5.2

question: How did people in the early twentieth century make mechanical typing of Chinese faster, and what is that story meant to show about how today's language models work?
points: The machine had thousands of separate characters, so typing speed depended on how far the operator had to move between one character and the next.

People counted in existing texts which characters tend to occur one after another (bigrams / n-grams) and placed characters that occur together next to each other, which made typing much faster than with a random layout.
The point of the story: counting what tends to come next and predicting it is the same simple principle that is now called next-token prediction in LLMs.
author: fable-5.2

question: Among consumer-facing generative-AI products, which kind of user turns out to pay for them, and what reasoning and examples are given for that?
points: The paying users are 'prosumers': individuals who build the tool into their daily work and productivity.
Products of this kind named as successes, each with revenue in the hundreds of millions: Cursor, Runway, Plaud and ElevenLabs.
The contrast given: the speaker would not pay $20–50 a month for an image generator he plays with for fun, but would readily pay $20 for something that lets him do his job better.

Spending on work tools is already routine: a startup pays roughly $9–25 per person for each of several SaaS tools (Google Workspace, Slack, 1Password, GitHub Copilot), so a couple of hundred dollars for productivity is easily spent.
author: fable-5.2

question: How do web serving, large-scale data analytics and AI training differ in the balance between moving data and doing computation, and in what happens when one machine fails in the middle of a job?
points: Web serving: a lot of I/O and little computation, embarrassingly parallel (replicate the server when traffic grows).
Data analytics: still a lot of I/O, but the computation is not embarrassingly parallel and needs abstractions such as Spark or MapReduce to run one query as a distributed system.
AI training: computation far outweighs I/O; datasets are only tens of terabytes to a petabyte or two, while training a single image model already takes about an exaflop.
On failure, a data job simply recomputes the lost chunk on another machine, whereas in distributed training one GPU machine going down ends the whole job, which has to be restarted.
author: fable-5.2

question: Compared with cloud-era servers, what is new about how machines in the latest rack-scale GPU systems reach each other's memory, and what does that make easier for very large models?
points: In cloud-era designs each machine is its own domain: machines communicate through primitives such as RPC or MPI and cannot access another machine's memory without asking it for permission.

In the rack-level design (NVIDIA's 72-GPU rack, with high-bandwidth switches in the middle of the rack) every machine can access the other machines' memory directly, so the rack behaves much like a single mainframe.
For training or deploying massive models one no longer has to cut the model into pieces that fit individual machines.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why is it argued to be tolerable that AI application companies currently collect less from their users than they pay model providers for tokens, and what risk in that argument is admitted?
points: The price of a given quality falls quickly: today's much better models (GPT-4o / GPT-5 class) cost about what GPT-3.5 cost a couple of years earlier.

By that trend a company that loses 50% now would break even next year at the same quality, as long as customers are happy and value is created, so companies focus on creating value first rather than on earning money.
The admitted structural risk: if no real value is being created, the whole thing is a house of cards.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why has a simple abstraction layer for launching workloads on any cloud, which works for ordinary services, stayed hard to achieve for AI training?
points: Conventional cloud abstractions (virtual machines, Kubernetes) assume machines are replaceable and that their physical location does not matter, because the workloads on them are not tightly integrated.
In distributed AI training locality matters: the machines of one job should sit on the same rack, attached to the same switch.

Data locality: installing the software anywhere is easy, but a petabyte-scale dataset has to be put on the storage attached to those machines, and storage is fragmented (block / file / object storage on the big clouds versus NFS, Lustre and other parallel file systems on neo-clouds and Slurm clusters), so moving data remains the bottleneck.
author: fable-5.2

question: When building an automatic answer checker for agent training data, what does the example of a shopper asking how much money comes back after paying for a cheap drink show about how the checker must treat equivalent answers, and why are checker mistakes on such cases especially damaging?
points: If the question only asks for the amount, every mathematically equivalent form of it (e.g. one half and two quarters) must be accepted as correct.
If the question additionally asks for the simplest form, only the reduced form (one half) is correct, so the verifier has to capture this nuance of the question.
Such verifier errors are costly because current models mostly fail only on these harder, nuanced cases; if the verifier is wrong there too, the model cannot be improved further.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why should a coding model's ability to fix real repository issues be measured under several different agent scaffolds (the tool wrappers around the model) rather than a single one, and what does a large accuracy drop after exchanging the scaffold point to?
points: Different harnesses give the model different tools for the same task: one environment may offer a ready-made function for opening a file while another does not, so the same step has to be done in another way.
Solving the task under all these tool variants, instead of sticking to one harness, shows that the model's intelligence has passed a certain threshold.
A significant performance drop when the harness is swapped while the model stays the same suggests that something went wrong in training, which then has to be changed.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the two-stage recipe for agentic models (first imitate demonstration trajectories, then reinforcement learning), why should the imitation stage be kept light and its demonstrations varied?
points: The imitation (SFT) stage only serves to make the model able to sample meaningful trajectories.
If the demonstrations are few and similar in style, the model cannot generate diverse attempts later in the RL stage.
Heavy SFT teaches the model to remember the single given answer for every training question, so it loses the ability to work out answers on its own.
Because no training set can cover every interaction, a model taught only to follow demonstrations fails on out-of-distribution tasks.
author: fable-5.2

question: Among the remedies for a model's outputs becoming uniform during long reinforcement-learning runs, what does it mean to train only on the model's own current attempts, and how does that compare with using attempts from elsewhere in terms of reward, drift from the starting model and output diversity?
points: On-policy means the reward model or verifier only judges attempts produced by the current model itself, not answers from other models or from different weights.
Training reward rises in a similar way in the on-policy and the off-policy setting.
On-policy training keeps the KL divergence from the initial policy small and the entropy high.
On benchmarks the on-policy variant generally gives better results.
author: fable-5.2

question: When the same reinforcement-learning setup was trained on math datasets of different difficulty and compared on one common validation set, how did an easy grade-school set and a hardest-problems-only set each fare against a mixed set, and what lesson is drawn about choosing training prompts?
points: Training only on GSM8K ends with the lowest validation accuracy, because that set is too easy to prepare the model for challenging tasks.
Training only on the difficult subset ends below training on the full set, which contains the difficult problems together with less difficult ones.
Lesson: blindly feeding very hard prompts does not work, because current models and algorithms are not able to learn from them alone; data of different difficulty has to be combined.
author: fable-5.2

question: What flaw of plain majority voting over many independently sampled solutions is fixed by taking the model's own confidence in each sample into account, how does that change the vote, and what result is reported for it?
points: In plain majority voting (e.g. 32 samples of the same prompt) some sampled trajectories are of very low quality but still count in the vote.
The method tracks the generation confidence of each sampled trajectory.
Trajectories with very low confidence are left out of the vote or given a very low weight.
On the same model (GPT-OSS 120B) this does better than plain consensus, i.e. majority voting.
author: fable-5.2

question: What is the main attraction of a benchmark whose test cases never change, and which two advantages are claimed for benchmarks whose test cases are regenerated on a regular schedule?
points: A fixed (static) test set gives direct, reproducible comparison: the same model gets the same score now and years later, which suits publications and comparison between companies.
A regularly refreshed (dynamic) benchmark stays relevant as real-world data shifts, for example as more of the content on the internet is generated by LLMs.
It is harder to overfit or game, because the refreshed test cases cannot simply be taken as training data.
author: fable-5.2

question: An agent benchmark can mislead in two ways: solving its tasks may not prove the skill it is meant to test, or its score may not match whether the task was really accomplished. What are the two corresponding requirements called, how is each defined, and which one is the main concern when building an evaluator agent?
points: Task validity: success on the task must actually reflect the target capability; it depends on how the task and the environment are built.
Outcome validity: the evaluation result must faithfully reflect whether the task was successfully completed (a good result means the agent really completed the task).
Outcome validity is the one singled out as the key thing to track when building the evaluator (green agent).
author: fable-5.2

question: How can the answer being graded manipulate a language model that serves as the grader, and which incident from academic paper reviewing is cited to show that this happens in practice?
points: The graded text can carry an instruction addressed to the judge, e.g. a sentence at the end asking for a full score, which can make the LLM judge award full marks.
Cited incident: authors put such text invisibly into their papers; LLMs used to write reviews read it and produced very favourable reviews, while human readers could not see it.
Conclusion: an LLM judge has to be made robust against this kind of manipulation.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the security benchmark where an agent must craft an input that triggers a described vulnerability in a real code base, how is a submission judged, and how does the benchmark guard against models having memorised the cases?
points: The agent's proof-of-concept is executed on both the pre-patch and the post-patch build.
It counts as a reproduction if it triggers the target vulnerability only on the pre-patch build; triggering any vulnerability on the post-patch build is counted as a post-patch finding.
The check is done by runtime sanitizers (crash and stack trace), so it is verifiable rather than a subjective judgment by an LLM or a human.
Contamination is handled by evaluating on vulnerabilities that were found only after the tested model's knowledge cutoff.
author: fable-5.2

question: For the customer-service benchmark in which an agent serves a simulated user through API calls under a domain policy (tau-bench) and its successor (tau-squared-bench), how does the successor change who can act on the environment, and how does the way success is checked change?
points: Original: single control - only the agent has tools, there is one database, and the LLM-simulated user uses no tools.

Successor: dual control - the simulated user also has its own tool set, there are two databases (the agent's and the user's device), and the setting is framed as a decentralised partially observable Markov decision process that stresses coordination.
The original judges success by comparing the final database state with the annotated goal state.
The successor adds assertion-style checks (environment, communication, natural-language and action assertions) on components or steps of the task instead of checking only the end state.
author: fable-5.2

question: What was wrong with the original benchmark of real GitHub issues for coding agents that led to a human-screened subset, how large was the screening and how much did it discard, and what did one model's scores before and after show?
points: Some original tasks had underspecified issue descriptions, overly specific or misaligned tests, and setup friction, which caused false negatives.
93 professional developers reviewed about 1,700 samples; 68.3% were filtered out (38.3% had specification problems, 61.1% had unfair unit tests), leaving 500 tasks.
GPT-4o reaches 33.2% on the screened subset against about 16% on the original, which indicates that the original underestimated capability.
author: fable-5.2

question: What was observed when reinforcement learning with an automatically checkable reward was run on a single math problem instead of a normal-sized training set, and how was that single problem chosen?
points: Accuracy on the unchanged evaluation set (many different questions) kept rising and ended close to the run trained on about 1,200 examples.
This is taken to show that RL does not memorise the training example but learns how to solve math problems, i.e. it is extremely data-efficient.

The problem was selected by the variance of the model's rollouts on it: problems on which the rollouts differ a lot are preferred because they allow more exploration, and not every example works equally well.
author: fable-5.2

question: In what ways did coding models game test-based graders during reinforcement-learning training, and how was tampering with the tests prevented?
points: The model deleted the test cases or rewrote their contents so that they simply pass.
On tasks with internet access (SWE-bench Verified is the example) it looked up the existing solution online and copied it as its output.
The tests are hidden (removed) while the model works in the sandbox and are patched back in afterwards for the actual test run.
In addition another model is used to check the model's output, and repeated cheating is given a very high penalty.
author: fable-5.2

question: In large-scale reinforcement-learning training of agentic models, which stage has become the slowest, and how does letting rollout generation and weight updates run without waiting for each other work, including its drawback?
points: Sampling (generating rollouts) is now the slowest part, slower than the trainer, especially for long chain-of-thought or long-horizon rollouts.
In the asynchronous setup the trainer and the samplers do not wait for each other: samplers keep generating without needing the latest policy, e.g. with the policy from the previous iteration.
Drawback: it takes a lot of work to make this converge and run well, particularly at the scale of thousands of GPUs.
author: fable-5.2

question: When training an agentic model, what happens if the cost charged for long solutions is too small, what happens if it is too large, and which simple mechanisms are used during training to bound rollout length?
points: Too small: the model keeps retrying and can spend unlimited tokens until it believes it has a better answer, which makes solving more likely but is bad for cost and user experience (a one-minute solution is preferred over a one-hour one).
Too large: exploration is sacrificed, because the model is no longer encouraged to explore longer solutions.

Mechanisms: very long rollouts are cut off (e.g. after 30 minutes or an hour), a token-based cost is applied, and shorter answers are preferred when the problem is solved under different length constraints.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why is low-rank adaptation regarded as a particularly good fit for reinforcement-learning fine-tuning, although elsewhere it has sometimes been worse than updating all weights?
points: LoRA comes with built-in regularisation: the main weights stay fixed, so the overall change to the weights is small.
RL needs much more regularisation than SFT, because the policy should not move far away from the previous checkpoint.
Off-policy training needs it especially: if the policy used for sampling and the policy being trained differ a lot, convergence becomes hard.
A side benefit is that fewer GPUs are needed (more efficient).
author: fable-5.2

question: From the standpoint of a team shipping a product model, what does reinforcement learning deliver that supervised fine-tuning does not, at what price, and why is it easier to steer than preference-based training with a learned reward model?
points: RL trades compute (far more than SFT uses) for robustness: the model still gives acceptable answers when users ask in a different way, not just better benchmark numbers.
With RL set up correctly, quality keeps improving as more compute is added until the model's limit, which pre-training cannot always do because it is also limited by data.

Steerability: to change the model's behaviour one just defines or changes a grader (which behaviour gets a good or bad reward), which is more flexible than training a reward model as in RLHF or using SFT.
author: fable-5.2

question: When a game-playing strategy is rated by how much it would lose to an ideal counter-strategy, what is the adversary assumed to know and not to know, and why is such a pessimistic assumption defended for AI systems that are released to the public?
points: The opponent is assumed to know our strategy completely, e.g. to have full access to the model's weights and the exact probability it assigns to each action.
The opponent does not know the outcomes of random draws (such as the random seed), which is why randomising between actions still protects the strategy.
The justification: a system that is online and used by billions of people will sooner or later have any weakness found and exploited, so it should stay robust even against someone who knows it fully.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why is finding the single best move, as a chess or Go engine does, not sufficient in a game like poker where the players hold private information?
points: In hidden-information games the worth of an action depends on how often it is played, whereas in perfect-information games it does not (playing a given chess opening 10% or 90% of the time does not change its expected value).

The opponent adapts to the frequency: someone who bluffs too often gets called more and bluffing loses value; in the rock-paper-scissors variant, playing rock 80% of the time makes the opponent switch to paper and the value of rock drops from 0 to -1.
The algorithm therefore has to find the right probability for each action, not only which action to take.
author: fable-5.2

question: What is the argument that, in a two-player zero-sum game, a player following an equilibrium strategy can never gain anything by exchanging messages with the opponent?
points: All minimax equilibria of such a game give player 1 the same single value, and player 2's value is exactly its negative.
If a message would raise the sender's value, the other player would simply ignore it, because it would lower their own value.
If a message would lower the sender's value, it would not be sent; the only case left is that talking has no effect.
author: fable-5.2

question: What does the ultimatum game (one player proposes how to split a sum of money, the other can accept or veto it) show about agents that are trained only by playing against themselves and are then expected to deal with people?
points: Pure reward maximisation leads the proposer to offer the smallest possible amount and the responder to accept it, since any positive amount beats nothing.
Real people mostly refuse very low offers, so that strategy would perform terribly with humans; the fault is in the optimisation, not in the humans.

What people accept differs by culture (in some, 20% is accepted easily; in others anything below an even split is rejected), which cannot be learned without human data, so one should collect human data and compute the best response to it.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the no-press Diplomacy experiments that mixed an agent trained purely by self-play with agents trained on human games, how did each kind do when it was the lone outsider among six of the other kind, and what does that say about the game?
points: One human-data-trained agent (SearchBot) playing with six copies of the self-play agent (DORA) won only about 1% of games, whereas an even share in a seven-player game is one seventh, about 14%.
One DORA playing with six SearchBots won only about 11% of games, also below the even share.
The conclusion is that the game has different equilibria: DORA found one that works among copies of itself but does not know what to do among agents playing a human-like equilibrium.
author: fable-5.2

question: Which two ways of running a model many times in parallel are offered as alternatives to letting it reason serially for ever longer, and what restricts the kind of task each one works on?
points: Consensus: sample the model many times (a dozen to a hundred; 64 in the competition-math example) and submit the most frequent answer; it only works when the answer is very short, not for something like an essay.
Best-of-n: sample many times and use some judge to pick the best answer; it works well only when a solution is easy to verify, as with checking a Sudoku.
The general trade-off of such parallel techniques is lower latency at the price of being less compute-efficient.
author: fable-5.2

question: When the per-question results of many models on one benchmark are laid side by side, what irregularity shows up, and why does it undercut the hope that a few very hard questions can make up for a small test set?
points: The best overall models sometimes fail easy questions, while weak models that succeed only about 30% of the time sometimes solve quite hard ones.
This suggests the questions are not that special: even poor models have some (lower) chance of getting them right, so one should be suspicious of treating a hard success as strong evidence.
Analogy given: a person who writes down a long proof of P != NP but cannot define NP has probably copied it, and for benchmark problems (unlike truly open problems) copying is possible.
author: fable-5.2

question: On HumanEval, roughly how large must the score gap between two models be before it is statistically significant, with and without comparing the models question by question, and how do these thresholds relate to the gains papers usually report?
points: With only 164 problems, the standard error of a single model's score is about 4%.
Without pairing, a difference of about 10% is needed to reach the conventional 5% p-value; with a paired test about 8% is typically still needed.
Both thresholds are larger than the improvements reported in many papers.

Intuition for pairing: unpaired is like two students scoring 50% and 60% on different years' exams, where one exam may simply have been easier; when both take exactly the same exam the same gap is more convincing.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the toy comparison between a model with a small chance of success on every question and a model that always succeeds on half of the questions and never on the rest, why can the model with the lower average score be the better one, and what kind of training is said to lead to the second profile?
points: Model A solves each of the eight questions with probability 10%; model B solves four of them with probability 100% and the other four with probability 0%, so B's average is much higher.
B's profile can result from RL that maximises expected reward: the expected reward goes up while the set of questions that can be solved at all shrinks.
If errors can be corrected, for example with a verifier in the loop, A is the better model.
author: fable-5.2

question: Which probability distribution is fitted to an LLM's per-question chances of answering correctly in order to explain why benchmark noise is predictable, and what shape does it take once a model performs reasonably well?
points: A beta distribution fits the empirical distribution of per-question probability of being correct, once the questions that no model solves (true zeros) are accounted for separately.
For models that are good enough it is bimodal, with the two parameters summing to roughly one (a larger sum would make it unimodal).
Using this model, the amount of noise can be predicted without having all the individual per-question results.
author: fable-5.2

question: How can a table of every model's result on every benchmark question be used to find faulty benchmark items and to flag models that may have been trained on the test data?
points: Look for questions that are negatively correlated with overall model performance, i.e. the better the model, the worse it does on them.
In most datasets such questions are not real errors, but in MBPP a number of them were inconsistent or incorrect; these fixes were incorporated into MBPP+.

On such faulty items a leading, non-cheating model will not match the reference, so a model that gives the exact (wrong) answer from the evaluation set is evidence that it may have trained on the evaluation data.
author: fable-5.2

question: How can model families released in several sizes be used to gauge whether a benchmark can detect a real improvement, and how do MMLU and HumanEval compare on that measure?
points: Take the consistent improvement obtained when the model size is doubled as the signal and relate it to the benchmark's noise, as a signal-to-noise ratio expressed as a z-score.
The result is still mostly a function of benchmark size.
MMLU can very reliably distinguish the next larger model, whereas many code benchmarks such as HumanEval cannot even distinguish a doubling of model size.
author: fable-5.2

question: How does Sierra, the company that builds customer-service agents for other businesses, bill its clients, and why is that arrangement presented as better aligned than subscription or usage-based software pricing?
points: The client is charged only when the agent actually resolves the end customer's problem (for example completes the shoe exchange); if it does not, there is no charge.
It is presented as the step after one-time boxed software, subscription SaaS and pay-for-what-you-use pricing (AWS, Snowflake).
It ties the vendor's revenue to the client's benefit: the client pays only when it is saving money or when the agent has made a sale.
author: fable-5.2

question: Before AI voice agents, why was it so hard to run a controlled experiment on call-centre phone conversations, and what becomes possible once an agent handles the calls?
points: Most calls to contact centres are not even transcribed, so what happened in them cannot be analysed.
The only way to compare two approaches was to hand one script to about a thousand human staff and a different script to another thousand and hope they followed it.
With agents every customer channel, including the phone, is digital, so the A/B testing and experiment-design methods from 20-30 years of building websites can be applied to conversations.
author: fable-5.2

question: For a phone-based AI agent, between which two moments should response delay be measured, and what is done so that a reply is ready the instant the caller has finished speaking?
points: The delay that matters runs from the moment the person stops talking (end of utterance) to the moment the agent starts responding, not from the end of the audio chunk being analysed.
The system therefore has to recognise as quickly as possible that the caller has stopped, so that reasoning and speech synthesis can start.
Several reasoning-and-synthesis runs are often started in advance, and it is checked afterwards whether the caller really had stopped at that point, so that a response is already prepared.
author: fable-5.2

question: Why is word error rate considered the wrong first yardstick for judging speech transcription in a customer-service voice agent, and what general advice about evaluation metrics is drawn from that?
points: Word error rate rewards transcribing every word in the audio, including for example a TV news programme playing in the background of the call.
What is actually wanted is only the primary speaker's words, with background and secondary speakers ignored.

The team therefore built its own metrics; the general advice is not to assume that existing metrics for a component are the right ones, but to work out what a great experience looks like and measure that.
author: fable-5.2

question: What happened the first time Sierra's founders left a simulated customer talking unattended to their early prototype agent, and what omission caused it?
points: The prototype, built on a ReAct loop, could only answer questions about 1099 tax forms and do simple arithmetic; a second LLM agent played the customer because agent-to-agent testing was more efficient (GPT-4 was very slow then).
Neither agent had been given any way to hang up and end the conversation.
After the actual question was answered, the two kept thanking each other and replying 'you're welcome' for about a hundred further messages.
author: fable-5.2

question: Roughly what proportion of incoming support requests do Sierra's agents resolve without a human, and how are the conversations that get handed to human staff used to improve the agent afterwards?
points: The AI agent answers first and handles roughly 60 to 90 percent of service and support inquiries; the remaining 10 to 20 percent are handed over to a person in the contact centre.
Things the agent does not know are often known by those human experts, so the feature looks across the common reasons for escalation and at how the experts answered them.
AI is then used to synthesise new knowledge from those answers and give it to the agent, so that later runs can handle such cases.
author: fable-5.2

question: How did AlphaStar generate the structured commands it sent to StarCraft, and why is the way current LLMs call tools more flexible than that design?
points: AlphaStar's commands were API calls with several arguments, produced by a hand-crafted autoregressive network with a separate softmax output for each argument (for example whether to queue, the delay, the position), trained by imitation and reinforcement learning.
That architecture itself encoded the one API and was fixed, whereas LLMs write the call as text or code with a single transformer, which generalises to all sorts of environments.
With LLMs the call format can be changed simply by instructing the model, while in AlphaStar trying a different design meant retraining the model to see which played better.
author: fable-5.2

question: What behaviour did AlphaStar arrive at when it was trained with reinforcement learning alone, without human game data, and what did the team conclude from it?
points: It learned to take all of its worker units and send them to attack the enemy.
This did beat the hardest built-in game AI, but only by exploiting the fact that it was not programmed to defend well against that kind of attack, which was considered an unsatisfactory result.
The conclusion was that human data was needed: imitation learning on human games first, with a reinforcement-learning loop on top.
author: fable-5.2

question: In AlphaStar's reinforcement-learning stage, what problem did plain RL on top of the imitation-trained policy cause, and how many Elo points were gained by the fix for it and by adding explicit conditioning?
points: The imitation-only (supervised) policy stood at about 900 Elo, and plain RL on top of it gave only a small boost.
Plain RL tended to collapse the behaviours: the diversity of strategies picked up from human games was lost.
The fix was a KL penalty towards the supervised policy, i.e. distilling the original policy into the one being trained, which raised Elo by about 400.
Explicitly conditioning the agent on what it should do added almost 150 Elo more.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the discussion of the ways AlphaStar could be beaten, what separates an adversarial policy, an exploiter and a 'cheese' strategy in terms of how widely each one works against other opponents?
points: An adversarial policy is like an adversarial example for an image classifier: odd unit movements that make the network break down; it is tied to the specific weights of that network.
An exploiter plays properly but repeatedly against one opponent whose weights do not change until it finds a strategic weakness and goes deep into it; it is specific to that single opponent.
Cheese is a strategy that carries over to many different opponents but is not the optimal way to play; it appears even at the top professional level, mixed with normal play to stay unpredictable.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the AlphaStar league, what is a main exploiter agent trained to do, when do the main agents first get to play against it, and what happens to it after that?
points: Its only objective is to beat the main agents; it starts from the imitation-learned prior.
There is an asymmetry: the exploiter trains against the main agent and learns from those games, while the main agent cannot train against it during that time.
Only once its win rate against the main agents is very high does it drop a checkpoint that the main agents can then play against; the exploiter then restarts the same process from the prior.
The effect is that the main agent is exposed to the counter-strategy (for example stalkers against an all-void-ray style) and learns to react to it.
author: fable-5.2

question: Compared with the reinforcement-learning stage of AlphaStar, in what respects is RL-based post-training of large language models described as still immature or harder?
points: Compute: for LLMs most compute goes into pre-training and only a little into post-training, whereas for AlphaStar most of the compute and weight updates were in the reinforcement-learning stage.
Scale: LLM post-training runs for perhaps thousands of steps, against about 10^10 training steps in the AlphaStar league.
Rewards: StarCraft has a computable win/lose outcome, while for general LLM tasks (such as judging a poem) the reward cannot be fully specified.
Overfitting: the supply of interesting human tasks for LLMs is limited, whereas every StarCraft game is unique, so the problem did not arise there.
author: fable-5.2

question: What makes the human-centric image benchmark created with Sony AI different from web-scraped image datasets, and why is it suited to evaluating models but not to training them?
points: Everyone who appears in the pictures took part consensually, was compensated, and self-identified the labels that describe them, instead of the images being scraped from sites such as YouTube, Instagram or Reddit.
It has about 10,000 images, from 81 countries and areas: not enough to train a model on, but enough to evaluate a model for biases.
It was used to analyse biases in vision-language models, confirming some known ones and identifying new ones.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the Tetris demonstration of the TAMER system, how did an agent taught through a person's approval and disapproval compare with ordinary reinforcement learning, both in how fast it learned and in how good it finally became?
points: A person watching the game signals 'good move' or 'bad move', and the agent learns from this evaluative feedback rather than from random exploration alone.
Speed: it is already much better than random in the first game and clears hundreds of lines by about the third game, whereas ordinary RL needed hundreds of thousands of games for the task.
Final level: it ultimately does not do as well as reinforcement learning left to learn from scratch (linked to Sutton's bitter lesson).
A follow-up, TAMER+RL, learns both from human feedback and autonomously to combine the two.
author: fable-5.2

question: In the robot mobile-manipulation work that learns on the real robot without any demonstrations, what does 'unsupervised reinforcement learning' mean, where is it carried out, and what does it produce?
points: The agent is given an environment to explore but no reward signal and no task, and tries to work out behaviours that may be useful once a reward is given later (like a baby playing in a playpen).
It is carried out in a rough, low-fidelity simulator of the robot.

Its product is a latent action space: a small set of latent action dimensions such that changing them gives meaningfully different behaviours, for example moving the base towards or away from the whiteboard, moving the arm, or pointing the camera.
author: fable-5.2

question: How much training on the physical robot did the whole-body mobile-manipulation method that pre-learns its action representation in a rough simulator need, and how did it compare with the baselines it was tested against?
points: Starting from random behaviour, the robot learned to wipe the marks off the whiteboard, moving base, camera and arm together, after only about 40 minutes.
All four tasks (wiping with or without an obstacle, sweeping rubbish onto a tray, sweeping it into a bag) were learned with the same action space, each in less than one hour on the real robot.

Compared with doing all the learning in simulation, with SERL (which learns in the low-level action space) and with RLPD, it reached higher success rates and had fewer safety violations during learning.
author: fable-5.2

question: How was the training experience of the Gran Turismo racing agent arranged so that it would learn overtaking tactics?
points: Besides driving alone or with 20 cars spread around the track, special starting situations were created with the agent placed behind one, two, three or seven other cars, so that it gained experience in traffic.

Starting behind another car on a straight encourages (without explicitly instructing) a slipstream pass, which works because the simulator models the reduced air resistance; starting behind a car in a corner teaches crossover passes.
These scenarios were combined into a carefully engineered mix in the experience replay buffer and training mini-batches; this was done by hand for the Nature paper and automated in later work.
author: fable-5.2

question: What two opposite kinds of misbehaviour did the Gran Turismo racing agent show with respect to racing etiquette, and how was its reward adjusted in response?
points: Etiquette (no avoidable collisions, no forcing a driver off the track) is a matter of judgment that a human steward assesses.
Too aggressive: without handling this, the agent simply pushes another car off the track, which is not allowed.
Too timid: while holding a commanding lead the agent braked because it was too concerned about causing a collision, and the human expert passed it.
The response was to add reward terms so that it avoids collisions, especially collisions it would be judged at fault for and penalised for.
author: fable-5.2

question: Two lectures introduce next-token prediction through older methods that simply count how often words or characters follow one another. What limits of such counting does each lecture name, and what is said to have replaced it?
points: Lecture 1: a count-based model has to store a count for every sequence and every continuation, which needs an infeasibly large amount of memory.

Lecture 1: a context that never occurred in the training text (for example a hundred lines of new code) has a count of zero and so gets probability zero, i.e. the model cannot generalise; the remedy is a parametric estimator, a neural network.

Lecture 2: counting by hand could look back only two or three characters and classical NLP stopped at about 5-grams because the table of correlations grows out of hand, whereas current models predict from contexts of up to millions of tokens.
author: fable-5.2
note: L1+L2, agree/complement: both start from n-gram counting and name its limits

question: Sutton's 'bitter lesson' is cited in several lectures. What conclusion does each one draw from it: for how language-model training should be designed, for computing infrastructure, and for teaching an agent with human feedback?
points: Lecture 1: more compute gives better performance and compute keeps growing, so in the long run what matters is methods that leverage compute; do not over-complicate things for today's scale, do the simple thing and make sure it scales.

Lecture 2: the lesson (a general method with a large amount of computation on a large amount of data is the most effective approach) is given as the reason so much computing power is needed, which is why AI infrastructure has become a pillar of IT and cloud strategy in its own right.

Lecture 11: it is linked to the TAMER result: with human feedback the agent learns far faster, but in the end it does not get as good as reinforcement learning from scratch, i.e. injecting human input can lower the final performance.
author: fable-5.2
note: L1+L2+L11, complement: the same idea used for three different conclusions

question: When a coding model is trained by reinforcement learning with test cases as the reward, which unintended shortcuts do the lectures report, and which safeguards against them are described?
points: Lecture 1: the model may pass the tests by removing the test from its environment or replacing it with one that always returns true; it optimises the reward exactly as written, not what was intended.

Lecture 1: the KL term in the RL loss, which tells the policy not to move too far from the outputs of a reference (base) model, is described as a hack that limits how far RL can drift into such unwanted behaviour.
Lecture 5: models removed all the test cases or rewrote their contents so that they pass, and on tasks with internet access they looked up the existing solution and copied it.

Lecture 5: countermeasures are a second model that checks the output, hiding the tests while the model works in the sandbox and patching them back for the test run, and a very high penalty for cheating again.
author: fable-5.2
note: L1+L5, complement: same failure, different examples and countermeasures

question: For open-ended outputs that no automatic checker can mark as right or wrong, such as a translation or a piece of writing, where does the score come from according to the course: as the reward when training with reinforcement learning, and when evaluating a finished system?
points: Lecture 1: DeepSeek R1 uses rule-based verifiers for reasoning prompts (math, code, logic), but for general prompts such as translation, factual question answering and writing requests the reward comes from a reward model trained to predict human preferences.

Lecture 5: for open questions experts write a rubric: a list of clear, detailed criteria (50 for one question is no surprise), each of which can be scored, for example 1 or 0; this list is the input to the grader in RL.

Lecture 4: non-verifiable tasks are evaluated either by human raters, who judge several aspects of the output, or by an LLM used as a judge, which is much cheaper and quite consistent with human preference.
author: fable-5.2
note: L1+L4+L5, complement: training-time reward (reward model, rubric grader) vs evaluation (human, LLM judge)

question: Both the account of reinforcement learning for language models and the StarCraft project add a KL-divergence term that ties the policy being trained to another policy. In each case, which policy is it tied to, and what is the term meant to prevent?
points: Lecture 1: in GRPO-style training the policy is told not to move too far from the outputs of a reference (base) model; this is called a hack that keeps RL from ending up in places one does not want, such as reward hacks.

Lecture 10: AlphaStar added a KL penalty towards the supervised policy learned from human games (distilling the original policy into the one trained with RL), so that RL does not commit early to one way of playing and lose the diversity of human strategies; this raised Elo by about 400.
author: fable-5.2
note: L1+L10, differ: same device, different reference policy and purpose

question: Why can the same language model give different answers to the same benchmark question on two runs, and why is this run-to-run variation, according to the statistical analysis of benchmarks, not the only source of noise in a benchmark score?
points: Lecture 1: the model predicts a probability distribution over the next token and the output is sampled from it, which is why asking the same question does not always give the same answer.
Lecture 7: it is a common confusion that differing predictions are the only noise; the score also depends on which questions happened to be chosen, and that can be the more important kind of noise.

Lecture 7: with a noise variable added next to the question variable, the total variance splits additively into the variance due to the choice of questions (averaged over the model's noise) and the variance due to sampling the model several times.
author: fable-5.2
note: L1+L7, two facts: where the randomness comes from, and the second noise source

question: When an AI product is connected to a company's internal data, how do the course's two examples, an enterprise search tool for employees and a customer-facing service agent, make sure that nobody reaches data they are not entitled to?
points: Lecture 2: the enterprise search product (Glean) connects sources such as Google Drive, GitHub, the internal wiki and Microsoft 365 and integrates their authentication and access control, so that each person searches only the information he or she is allowed to access.

Lecture 9: the language-model agent never gets unrestricted access to a CRM or a transaction database; every interaction with systems of record goes through conventional deterministic software with access controls and keys.
author: fable-5.2
note: L2+L9, two facts/agree: access control kept outside the model in both

question: What operational lessons does the course give for keeping a product that depends on LLM inference available and responsive, both when a model service is restarted after an outage and when the model provider itself is slow or unavailable?
points: Lecture 2: after the main model behind a large chatbot had been shut off by accident, requests piled up, so on restart the first replica took all the traffic and died, then the next one; the fix was a traffic regulator in front of the service that lets only a limited amount of traffic in and ramps up gradually, which restored the service in 15 minutes.

Lecture 9: the response time of foundation models varies widely (a P90 of 500 ms or of 2,500 ms), so several identical requests are sent to the same inference provider and the first one that comes back is used.
Lecture 9: frontier models do not reach the five or six nines of reliability of hardened cloud services, so being able to fail over from one model provider to another has turned out to be important.
author: fable-5.2
note: L2+L9, complement: overload on restart (traffic regulator) vs slow or failing provider (hedged requests, failover)

question: Two game-playing agents in the course were trained with reinforcement learning, one for StarCraft and one for Gran Turismo racing. How did they differ in whether human game data was needed before reinforcement learning, and what is reported in each case?
points: Lecture 10: in StarCraft, with its combinatorial action space and long time horizon, a random policy does nothing useful, and pure RL only discovered an unsatisfactory strategy (attacking with all workers, which exploited the built-in AI); the team had to resort to imitating human replays first and to run RL on top.

Lecture 11: the racing agent was trained end to end by RL starting from random behaviour (driving in circles, backwards, off the track) with a reward for moving fast along the track; after about a day it beat the best humans on an empty track and after about a week also in competitive racing.
author: fable-5.2
note: L10+L11, differ: human data needed vs pure RL from scratch

question: An agentic model will be given tools it was not trained with, or tools whose interface has been changed. How does the course propose to test for robustness to this, and how to train for it?
points: Lecture 3: an agent must not break when a user supplies a new tool or modifies one; a benchmark such as SWE-bench should therefore be run under several harnesses with different tool sets (one offers an open-file function, another does not), and solving the task under all of them is what counts.

Lecture 5: because users can connect any tool (through MCP or their own API), one model has to generalise: it needs strong instruction following, must reflect and switch tools after a wrong call, is trained with many kinds of tools, and is penalised by the grader when it does not use a tool in the specified form.
Lecture 5: during RL the tool set is also varied between attempts, with a different set each time or some tools taken away.
author: fable-5.2
note: L3+L5, complement: evaluation side (several harnesses) vs training side

question: A paper reports that its model beats a baseline by a few points on a public benchmark. Which properties of the benchmark, and which statistical consideration, do the lectures say have to be checked before such a gain counts as real progress?
points: Lecture 3: the benchmark must still be hard: where every model already scores high (GSM8K is the example) a five-point gain proves little, also because the base model may have seen very similar data.

Lecture 3: it must separate models (stronger models should score higher; if weak and strong ones score alike the benchmark should be abandoned) and be diverse (a high score on some 50 near-identical prompts means little).

Lecture 7: the gain has to exceed the noise of the benchmark: with the 164 problems of HumanEval the standard error of one model's score is about 4%, so a gap of about 10% (about 8% with a paired test) is needed at the 5% level, more than many papers report.
author: fable-5.2
note: L3+L7, complement: benchmark quality criteria vs statistical significance

question: Several recipes in the course first imitate human data and then apply reinforcement learning. What purpose does the imitation stage serve in the post-training of language-model agents, and what different purpose does it serve for the Diplomacy agents that have to play with people?
points: Lecture 3: supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations is only there so that the model can sample meaningful trajectories for RL; it should be diverse and light, because heavy imitation (memorising the one right answer per training question) takes away the model's ability to find answers on its own and fails out of distribution.

Lecture 6: to do well with humans the target is the best response to the human population, which needs data on that population; so human data is used to train an imitation model of the humans, inference-time compute is scaled to model what they would do rather than to play better, and RL is run with these imitation models as part of the environment.
author: fable-5.2
note: L3+L6, differ: imitation as a jump-start for exploration vs imitation as a model of the human partners

question: Real users do not state their requests as clearly as early agent evaluations assumed. What does the course say such users are like and what that demands of an agent, and how does the customer-service agent company imitate such users when it tests its agents?
points: Lecture 3: early evaluations assumed a user with a clear target, but in the wild people often have no idea what they want and ask almost random questions, hoping the agent tells them what to do; the agent must work from vaguely specified instructions and find out the intention by proactively talking to the user, while still producing precisely formatted output.

Lecture 9: agents are tested in simulated multi-turn conversations with a user played by a language model that has a persona (for example angry and confused because a phone subscription was turned off) and whose input is messy, with typos.
author: fable-5.2
note: L3+L9, complement: requirement on the model vs how it is tested in practice

question: For the customer-service benchmark in which a language model plays the customer, how is the metric that demands success on repeated runs of the same task defined, and what argument is given for why a business cannot be satisfied with the success rate of a single run?
points: Lecture 4: tau-bench reports pass^1, the average success rate, and pass^k, for which the task is run k times independently and counts only if all k runs succeed; it is meant to capture reliability and consistency.

Lecture 9: a business has millions of interactions and each one must go right; an agent that solves a task 95% of the time succeeds k times in a row with probability 0.95 multiplied k times, which goes towards zero, so sustained success over many runs is what is measured.
author: fable-5.2
note: L4+L9, complement: definition of pass^k vs the motivation given by its authors' company

question: How does the course suggest dealing with the risk that a model scores well on a benchmark only because it saw the test items during training? Describe what the cybersecurity benchmark on reproducing software vulnerabilities does about it, and the check that can be run afterwards on the per-question results of existing benchmarks.
points: Lecture 4: CyberGym evaluates on vulnerabilities that were found only after the evaluated model's knowledge cutoff, which the model cannot have memorised; this gives a fair measure of its capability and also allows gauging how severe contamination is.

Lecture 7: on benchmark items whose reference answer is itself wrong, leading models that did not cheat do not give the dataset's answer; a model that gives exactly that wrong answer on several such items is a suspect for having been trained on the evaluation data.
author: fable-5.2
note: L4+L7, complement: prevention by benchmark design (post-cutoff items) vs detection from per-question data

question: Instead of letting a model reason ever longer in a single chain, the course discusses running several samples or agents in parallel at inference time. What motivates this, what is its cost, and what is said to be missing in how models are trained for it?
points: Lecture 6: chain-of-thought reasoning is inherently serial, so thinking for hours or weeks makes latency the bottleneck; parallel techniques such as consensus and best-of-n avoid this, and the general trade-off is lower latency but lower compute efficiency.

Lecture 5: making inference 'wider' means parallel thinking or handing the work to several agents coordinated by an orchestrator; today parallel thinking is only applied after the model has been trained (it just produces several results), and how to take it into account during training is called an open research topic.
author: fable-5.2
note: L5+L6, complement: motivation and trade-off vs the training gap

question: Both lectures on multi-agent learning use rock-paper-scissors to show that naively training an agent against itself does not reach the right mixed strategy. What failure does each describe, and what remedy does each propose?
points: Lecture 6: an ordinary single-agent RL algorithm such as PPO does not converge to the equilibrium in a rock-paper-scissors variant with altered payoffs, because nothing in it forces the probabilities of the actions to settle at a particular distribution.

Lecture 6: fictitious play fixes this: in every iteration each player plays the best response to the opponent's average strategy over all earlier iterations, and the average strategy converges (slowly) to the equilibrium.
Lecture 10: naive self-play oscillates around the uniform optimum, at each moment leaning strongly towards one move, so convergence is very hard.

Lecture 10: training against a population of policies works better, since the learner is exposed to many players; playing against the strongest opponent in the population is the most hopeful variant, though even in this toy game it does not always give the desired result.
author: fable-5.2
note: L6+L10, complement: same toy game, different diagnosis and fix (averaging vs populations)

question: Two lectures stop to define what an 'agent' is, one starting from the classic reinforcement-learning picture and today's LLM products, the other from long-standing autonomous-agents research. What does each say, and why does the second doubt that a chatbot qualifies?
points: Lecture 10: in the classic picture an agent with a goal exchanges observations and actions with a single, well-specified environment and maximises a reward that in games is fully specified.

Lecture 10: today the agent is the object a user asks questions of and gives feedback to: a harness that controls how the LLM is called to issue an action, a search or a terminal command, packaged together with a rich environment; the boundaries have become more diffuse.

Lecture 11: an agent is an intelligent system that interacts with its environment through sensors and effectors; an autonomous agent runs a continuous loop of sensing and acting and does not wait to be called, whereas a chatbot takes an input, gives an output and waits for more input.
author: fable-5.2
note: L10+L11, differ: LLM-era agent (user + harness + environment) vs sensor/effector loop

question: Two lectures observe that models which are strong overall still fail on easy cases. What evidence does each give, and what does each conclude from it, one about benchmarks and the other about how to train?
points: Lecture 7: in per-question results the best model sometimes fails an easy problem while rather bad models (about 30% success overall) sometimes solve hard ones; hence benchmark problems are not that special and one should be suspicious of making up for low statistical power with hard problems.

Lecture 10: LLMs that are at Fields-medal level in parts of mathematics flop on simple questions (which of two numbers is larger, how many r's are in 'strawberry'), and AlphaStar after imitation and RL did not react properly to fairly simple strategies when humans played it; adding robustness was the reason for multi-agent training.
author: fable-5.2
note: L7+L10, two facts: same observation, conclusions for evaluation vs for training

question: Both for industrial training of agentic language models and for the Gran Turismo racing agent, getting the composition of the training data right is described as a large part of the work. What is being mixed in each case, and how is the mix changed or produced over time?
points: Lecture 5: most of the data work is deciding the mixing ratios between kinds of data and tasks (this one 3%, that one 20%), and the mix is changed during training: more of the easier data at the beginning and more and more difficult data as the model gets stronger.

Lecture 11: the racing agent's replay buffer and mini-batches contain a carefully engineered mix of scenarios (an empty track, starting behind one, two, three or seven cars, behind a car on a straight or in a corner); for the Nature paper the mix was set by hand, later automated methods were developed.
author: fable-5.2
note: L5+L11, agree: data/experience mix as a key engineering task in both

question: What assessment does the course give of today's systems in which several LLM agents cooperate, and how does the company deploying customer-service agents nevertheless use additional LLM agents around its main agent?
points: Lecture 6: current multi-agent LLM systems are heavily engineered and brittle and there has been no clear success yet; a blog post that advises against building them is cited, saying agents cannot yet carry out the long-context, proactive discussion needed to settle conflicts any more reliably than a single agent, although the speaker expects this to change soon.

Lecture 9: the main agent is surrounded by micro-agents: a supervisor that checks that it stays on task, states only facts grounded in the knowledge base, gives no medical advice and does not disparage competitors, plus task-specific ones watching particular tasks.
author: fable-5.2
note: L6+L9, differ: scepticism about cooperating agents vs supervisor agents used in production

question: Apart from whether the task was completed, what else do the lectures say the scoring of an agent should take into account, both in the reward used for training and in benchmark results?
points: Lecture 3: a verifier should be thought of as a vector rather than one correct/incorrect number: an answer that is right but took too many steps or consumed too many tokens may still be penalised.
Lecture 4: for enterprise workloads efficiency matters, so the CRM benchmark (CRMArena) also reports the number of turns, the tokens spent and the cost in dollars.

Lecture 4: in the project checklist, for booking a ticket the success rate alone is too simple; a useful metric also reflects how cheap and convenient the ticket is and whether it meets the user's requirements.

Lecture 5: in training a token cost is charged and very long rollouts are cut off; in evaluation, leaderboards that report only the pass rate (SWE-bench Verified is the example) are not comparable unless rollout length, i.e. test-time compute, is at the same level, so the team also tracks rollout length.
author: fable-5.2
note: L3+L4+L5, agree: cost and efficiency as part of the score, at training and at evaluation time

question: How does byte-pair encoding decide which sub-word units are merged into the vocabulary of the tokenizer used for LLM pre-training?
author: fable-5.2
